children: 0944 ET - Major Gulf stock markets end lower Monday, with Saudi Arabia's Tadawul All Share Index falling 0.7%, while the Dubai Financial Market General Index and Abu Dhabi's benchmark index each loses 0.3%. The declines come as investors assess the prospect of further U.S. interest-rate increases following stronger-than-expected inflation data. Emirates NBD Research says higher borrowing costs could weigh more heavily on Saudi Arabia, where inflation remains below 2% and credit growth has slowed. In contrast, higher inflation and recovering lending activity in the U.A.E. could cushion the impact of tighter monetary policy, the bank says. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0929 ET - Higher interest rates are likely to weigh more heavily on Saudi Arabia's credit growth than the U.A.E.'s, Emirates NBD Research says. Saudi inflation remains below 2%, raising inflation-adjusted borrowing costs as lending growth slows. In contrast, higher U.A.E. inflation, partly reflecting more market-sensitive food and energy prices, has kept real borrowing costs lower, while credit growth has recovered from its spring slowdown. Both countries' dollar pegs require rates to broadly track U.S. policy. Emirates NBD expects another Federal Reserve rate increase this year, followed by a prolonged pause through much of 2027, leaving Saudi borrowers more exposed to tighter financial conditions. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0924 ET - Canada's September CPI report points to limited evidence that higher energy costs are spilling over to lift prices for myriad Canadian goods and services, says Karl Schamotta, chief market strategist at forex firm Corpay. Schamotta cites core-inflation data, which excludes volatile items like food and energy. Core prices decelerated in the month to 1.9% from 2% in August. The CPI report indicates a "still-weak domestic economy." Traders might reassess rate-policy expectations with the release later Monday of the BOC's quarterly business-outlook survey.(paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira)

0919 ET - Canada's inflation data for September suggest the Bank of Canada has wiggle room to wait on a possible interest-rate hike, says Andrew Grantham, economist at CIBC Capital Markets. Inflation in Canada accelerated to 3.1% on the strength of energy prices. Excluding gasoline, inflation rose 2.2%, or close to the BOC's 2% target, and the BOC's preferred measures of core inflation also slowed in September. Grantham says traders have priced in a greater likelihood of a rate increase next week, but the September data "suggests that there is little rush" to act. (paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira)

0916 ET - Canadian inflation heated up slightly last month, though there may still be reason for the Bank of Canada to remain calm. CPI rose 3.1% on-year in September after holding at 3% the month before, pushing above the top end of the central bank's 1%-3% target for the first time since May. The main driver as expected was energy prices, though headline inflation was a tick cooler than the 3.2% economists were expecting. Stripping out gasoline, inflation decelerated to 2.2% from August's 2.4%. The average of the Bank of Canada's preferred median and trim inflation measures averaged 1.85%, the coolest in six years. And the share of the CPI basket with annual inflation above 3% narrowed to 29.2% from 37.9% in August and 37.3% a year earlier. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

0909 ET - The dollar could lag many other G-10 currencies if AI concerns lead to further stock-market instability, ING's Francesco Pesole says in a note. "Stock-market turmoil is enough to drastically reduce Federal Reserve tightening plans, even with inflation running hot." This affects the dollar's safe-haven appeal. However, the dollar is unlikely to fall considerably despite, he says. The contagion of lower tech stocks to broader U.S and world equity indices has been contained, while Nasdaq falls look modest. The DXY dollar index could fall to 101.000 in coming weeks but not much further, he says. The DXY trades flat at 101.846 after reaching a two-week low of 101.576 Friday. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0906 ET - Bitcoin's role in an institutional portfolio is unaffected by short-term market noise, says Cartwright investment consulting director Sam Roberts. For many pension trustees and long-term institutions, the flagship cryptocurrency is unsuitable for long-term allocation, says Roberts. For those that do invest in it, the exposure should be small enough that a total loss wouldn't derail their objectives, while being re-balanced within the portfolio when needed, he says. Bitcoin is 2% higher at $82,501.(joseph.wilkins@wsj.com)

0845 ET - The euro's recent decline against the dollar looks overdone relative to underlying economic fundamentals, UBS Global Wealth Management strategists say in a note. "While stronger U.S. data, higher yields, and French fiscal concerns have supported the dollar, we believe markets have become excessively pessimistic on Europe, leaving room for [the euro to recover] toward our $1.16 year-end target." Europe's economy has remained resilient despite geopolitical tensions and elevated energy prices. While French fiscal risks remain a concern, a broader European debt crisis is unlikely, they say. The euro falls 0.3% to $1.1212, having reached a 17-month low of $1.1112 Wednesday, according to LSEG.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0840 ET - While France's fiscal crisis is likely to get worse before it gets better, the risk of contagion appears limited, Andrew Kenningham at Capital Economics says in a note. Exposure of French corporates and banks to sovereign bonds is relatively small, decreasing the chances of a domestic doom loop, he says. "Second, in contrast to the early 2010s, the ECB is now well placed to limit contagion," he says, noting its potential for bond or asset purchases if needed. Meanwhile, the deficits of other countries in the eurozone--which drove contagion in the early 2010s--remain stable, while political support for exiting the eurozone has declined. While a stand-off between France and the EU over fiscal policy could drive up spreads, an acute crisis remains a tail risk, Kenningham says. (don.forbes@wsj.com)

0752 ET - Cryptocurrencies rise as risk appetite recovers and seasonality suggests they should remain supported until year-end, IG analyst Chris Beauchamp says in a note. "Markets are probably bigger prisoners of seasonality than anyone would care to admit--the fourth quarter is a better time for stocks and cryptocurrencies, and while this year's worries are different to last year's, there is still plenty of weight left in the bullish case." U.S. earnings this week and next will, however, prove key along with oil prices for the performance of stocks and cryptocurrencies, he says. Bitcoin rises 1.6% to $82,212, according to LSEG. Ethereum rises 2.9% to $2,419.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0724 ET - Shares in French banks fall as part of a wider selloff in French assets after protests across the country turned violent at the weekend. Several protests over public school conditions and the government's planned budget-deficit cut deteriorated into rioting, against a backdrop of broader political and fiscal jitters that have already weighed on stocks. French bank stocks have been the European focus of a broader selloff in the sector as bond yields climb. A bond selloff cuts the market value of fixed income portfolios and increases borrowing costs. The 10-year French OAT yield increases 7.8 basis points to 4.866%. Shares in Societe Generale are down 2.8%, Credit Agricole is 2.5% lower and BNP Paribas falls 2.4%. (michael.hennessey@wsj.com)

0721 ET - It seems unlikely that the U.K. budget will deliver major new policy announcements, Investec analysts say in a note. There is little scope for large shifts in expenditure as the Iran conflict continues, and so focus is expected to be on short-term relief for households finances by modest rises in taxation, they say. Delaying major decision will give the government time to better assess spending priorities, while potentially removing the drag from higher energy costs if the war in Iran ends in the coming months, they say. "Decisions on major programs look delayed until next year and for his first budget we expect Mr Healey to follow the finance minister's equivalent of the Hippocratic oath, namely 'do no harm'." (don.forbes@wsj.com)
